slides.title: Modeling Geometries
slides.notes: Open the lecture by naming the change in question. Part I taught products and blades; Chapter 9 asks where those blades should live so that points, offset lines, cameras, distances, and motions become meaningful. Emphasize that pages 245-246 are a bridge into Part II rather than a long theorem section, so the deck is organized around design choices.

slides.title: A Geometry Is An Algebra Plus An Interpretation
slides.notes: Use this slide to slow down the word model. The chapter is not saying that every representation is equally good; it says each representation has a contract. If the embedding and metric do not make a product meaningful, the product should not be used as if it had Euclidean content. That framing will organize the later comparisons.

slides.title: Extra Coordinates Are Purchased Freedoms
slides.notes: Frame the four panels as four answers to one problem: how should familiar Euclidean objects be made native? Vector space keeps the original metric and is excellent for directions. Homogeneous coordinates buy offset incidence. Plucker coordinates specialize projective line reasoning. Conformal embedding spends two dimensions so the metric and Euclidean operators are built into the algebra.

slides.title: When Geometry Becomes A Zero Test
slides.notes: The point of this slide is to make incidence feel operational. In the homogeneous model, a line equation becomes a predicate and the meet of two lines gives a point whose residual can be checked. Plucker line coordinates extend this style to projective 3-D line geometry. Warn that a zero incidence test is not the same as a good Euclidean measurement.

slides.title: The Metric Decides What Products Can Measure
slides.notes: Explain the word budget literally: a model spends dimensions, signature choices, and implementation effort in exchange for native operations. The vector-space model has the Euclidean metric but no offset flats. Homogeneous geometry cheaply fixes offset incidence but does not give a full Euclidean geometric product. Conformal geometry costs more but lets distance and Euclidean motions become product-level statements.

slides.title: Tradeoffs Across Four Workhorse Models
slides.notes: Treat the table as a decision aid, not a universal ranking. A cheap vector-space model is best when the problem is directional. Homogeneous and Plucker models are strong when incidence dominates, especially for projective camera and line problems. Conformal geometry earns its larger representation when metric invariants, rounds, contact, and Euclidean motion composition are central.

slides.title: Chapter 9 Sets The Itinerary
slides.notes: Use the timeline to show that Chapter 9 is not isolated. It gives students a reading strategy for the next eight chapters. Chapter 10 keeps the original vector-space model honest. Chapters 11 and 12 build homogeneous and Plucker-style incidence tools. Chapters 13-16 move to conformal metric geometry. Chapter 17 returns to the design question.

slides.title: Ask For The Invariant Before The Coordinates
slides.notes: Turn this slide into a short design exercise. Ask students to imagine a ray tracer, a multi-camera calibration problem, and a rigid-body interpolation problem. Each task asks for different invariants, so it should not automatically use the same model. The strongest answer is the one where the native objects, metric, predicate, operator, chart risk, and validation check all fit together.

slides.title: Modeling Is The Bridge From Algebra To Geometry
slides.notes: Close by returning to the bridge idea. Chapter 9 is short, but it changes the reader's posture for the entire part. The algebraic machinery is not being replaced; it is being relocated into representation spaces where different geometric facts become native. That is why model selection is a computer science issue as much as a mathematical one.
